items.title: [0day] Bypassing Apple's System Integrity Protection
items.summary: The post presents a zero-day that bypasses Apple's System Integrity Protection by abusing the local OS upgrade process. It is a significant finding because SIP is a core protection against tampering with system files.
items.takeaway: Upgrade and installer paths often run with elevated trust and can be overlooked in security reviews. Defenders should treat OS update mechanisms as part of the attack surface.

items.title: From help desk impersonation to AD CS abuse: Investigating ESC1 and ESC8 intrusion paths
items.summary: Microsoft Threat Intelligence describes two intrusions where attackers impersonated help desk staff over Teams and used Quick Assist to gain interactive access. The attackers staged portable runtimes, performed discovery, then abused AD CS. In one case they used an ESC1 template to get privileged certificates and performed DCSync, and in the other they used PetitPotam and NTLM relay to ESC8 to obtain a domain controller certificate and authenticate via PKINIT. Defender containment blocked much activity in the first case, but a privileged identity excluded from automated containment remained a
items.takeaway: Automated containment is only as strong as its coverage, so any privileged identity exempted from it becomes the weak point. Relay attacks against AD CS web enrollment can be stopped by enforcing HTTPS and Extended Protection for Authentication.

items.title: Reversing to Engineer: Learning to 'Secure' XPC from a Patch
items.summary: The author reverses Apple's patch for the RootPipe issue to understand the underlying XPC flaw. That understanding is then used to harden the XPC service in the author's own tool, TaskExplorer. The write-up shows how a patch diff can expose the vulnerable pattern.
items.takeaway: A security patch is a map of the bug: diffing before and after reveals the vulnerable logic, which you can then check for in your own IPC code.

items.title: Block Blocking Login Items
items.summary: Apple changed how macOS stores login items, so the author shows how to parse the new files to detect persistence. The post is a practical guide to finding persistence in the updated format.
items.takeaway: Persistence detection depends on parsing the store the OS currently uses, so detection tooling must be updated whenever the storage format changes.

items.title: Escaping the Microsoft Office Sandbox
items.summary: The author describes gaining code execution through a malicious Word document, then escaping the Microsoft Office sandbox using a faulty regular expression. The escape is used to persist beyond the sandbox.
items.takeaway: Sandbox escapes often come from flawed input validation in policy or parsing logic rather than from the sandbox kernel itself. Test the rules that decide what is allowed, not just the isolation mechanism.

items.title: [0day] Abusing XLM Macros in SYLK Files
items.summary: The author reports a zero-day logic flaw in Microsoft Excel that enables code execution on macOS through malicious macros embedded in SYLK files. The attack uses the XLM macro mechanism.
items.takeaway: Attackers may hide macro execution in less common file formats that users and mail gateways do not expect, so file type handling is part of the attack surface.

items.title: Mass Surveillance, is an (un)Complicated Business
items.summary: The author reveals that a popular iOS app is a government surveillance tool. The analysis decrypts the app binary and studies its network traffic to show what it does.
items.takeaway: Decrypting App Store binaries and observing network traffic lets you verify what an app actually does, rather than relying on its stated behaviour.

items.title: Monitoring Process Creation via the Kernel (Part II)
items.summary: This part of the series examines using the macOS KAuth subsystem to monitor process creation in the kernel. It also covers the limitations of that approach, which matter when you rely on it for detection.
items.takeaway: A kernel-level event source can look authoritative, but its coverage gaps determine what a detection can actually see. Test what a monitoring hook misses before trusting it.

items.title: Monitoring Process Creation via the Kernel (Part III)
items.summary: This article explains how process creation events can be passed from kernel mode to user mode using the undocumented kev_msg_post function. It shows how an endpoint tool can get these notifications without relying on documented interfaces.
items.takeaway: Undocumented kernel interfaces can be the only route to telemetry, but they are fragile across OS versions. Reverse engineering them is useful, though the approach needs regular re-validation after updates.

items.title: [0day] Bypassing SIP via Sandboxing
items.summary: A guest post by CodeColorist describes a zero-day in which macOS sandboxing is abused to make a SIP-protected process load an untrusted library. The post highlights how security mechanisms can combine to undermine each other.
items.takeaway: Security features interact, and a restriction in one layer can be used to force behaviour in another. Threat models should consider how protections compose, not just how each one works alone.

items.title: How Deterministic SAST and AI Security Agents Divide the Work: Coverage, Harness Policy and Cost in Snyk VulnBench 2.0
items.summary: The authors benchmark nine SAST and AI security configurations on 108 attacker-reachable vulnerabilities in 20 web applications, crediting a finding only when it names both the source and sink within two lines. Snyk Code and Claude Code each found about 80% of the vulnerabilities, but they disagreed on many cases, and together they reached 101 of 108. The AI harness, including its built-in review policy, shaped what was missed as much as the underlying model did.
items.takeaway: Deterministic scanners and AI reviewers have complementary blind spots, so layering them is more effective than choosing one, and the harness wrapped around a model can matter as much as the model itself.

items.title: BUSTA: Teaching Small Language Models to Reason About Binary Execution
items.summary: The authors train small open models with reinforcement learning to predict the input register values that produce a given x86-64 basic block output state. Fine-tuning raises accuracy substantially, and the fine-tuned Nemotron-3-Nano comes within four points of frontier models at a far smaller parameter count. The training dataset and models are released.
items.takeaway: Reinforcement learning on a narrow, verifiable reverse engineering task can give a small model useful low-level reasoning, which suits resource-constrained analysis environments.

items.title: Pre-Crime for Agents, at the Last Second: Probing When a Recruited Agent Gives In
items.summary: The authors show that a linear probe on a target agent's activations can predict, before output is written, when the agent is about to leak a secret under peer pressure in a multi-agent setting. At a 5% benign flag rate it caught 82% of leaking calls, versus 26% for a zero-shot decision-model monitor. The probe also flags some permitted disclosures, and a simple bag-of-words classifier nearly matched it, so much of the gain comes from label training.
items.takeaway: Monitoring the internal state of an agent before it acts can catch a policy breach earlier than filtering its output, but a baseline text classifier may do nearly as well, so test against one before crediting the internals.

items.title: WebMaze: Defending Against LLM-Powered Web Scanners with Functionality-Coupled Deception
items.summary: WebMaze is a defence that embeds traps in real web pages and diverts LLM-based scanners into generated decoy sites while keeping genuine functionality intact. Across 12 applications and three scanners, decoy pages made up on average 93% of the distinct pages requested. Scanners still explored mostly decoys even when told about the mechanism and instructed to avoid it.
items.takeaway: Deception can be built into the application's own views so that automated LLM scanners waste their budget in decoy content without any harm to real users.

items.title: VeriCUA: Verification as Agentic Exploration for Computer-Using Agents
items.summary: The authors present VeriCUA, a platform-agnostic verifier for computer-using agents that builds a task rubric from the available context, then chooses GUI or code checks to gather evidence for unresolved requirements. Across online and offline settings it agrees better with reference labels than prior baselines, with the biggest gains on hard offline cases and stronger rejection of false completion claims. The analysis links these gains to complementary evidence sources and test-time exploration.
items.takeaway: A single observation channel, whether screenshots or program state, gives an incomplete picture, so verification improves when it actively gathers evidence from several independent sources and applies explicit rules for combining them.
